Let $F$ be a field, let $n\ge1$, and let the input be a valid $n\times n$ CSR
record as in [[def-csr-matrix-with-stored-entry-semantics]], representing
$A\in M_n(F)$. Matrix positions in this definition use one-based notation:
$(i,j)$ refers to CSR row $i-1$ and column index $j-1$. This row/column order
is fixed before the procedure begins; vector component label $i$ refers to
coordinate $i-1$. The procedure performs no pivoting or reordering. All field
operations below are exact.

Let $P=\{(i,j):a_{ij}\ne0\}$. Scan each row once to check the canonical and
increasing-index conditions and to record whether its diagonal position occurs.
If the input fails either pattern condition, return `invalid-pattern`. If a row
has no diagonal position, return `missing-diagonal(i)` for the least such $i$.

Copy the value in each input slot to a work array $W$, and regard the unit
diagonal of $L$ as implicit. Process rows $i=1,\ldots,n$ in increasing order.
For each $k<i$ with $(i,k)\in P$, in increasing $k$ order, do the following:

1. If $W_{kk}=0$, return `zero-pivot(k)`.
2. Set $W_{ik}\gets W_{ik}/W_{kk}$; this value is the stored factor $L_{ik}$.
3. Let $R$ be the increasing list of one-based matrix column labels $j>k$
   represented by row $i$'s CSR segment, and let $C$ be the corresponding
   increasing list represented by row $k$'s CSR segment. Set each pointer to
   the first entry of its list, or to
   that list's end marker when it is empty. While both pointers are within
   their lists, compare their current indices. If they are equal, call their
   common value $j$ and update
   $$W_{ij}\gets W_{ij}-W_{ik}W_{kj}$$
   and advance both pointers once. If the current index in $R$ is smaller,
   advance only its pointer once; if the current index in $C$ is smaller,
   advance only its pointer once, making no arithmetic update in either
   unequal-index branch. Stop when either pointer passes the end of its list.
   Do not skip a matching slot when a current work value is zero.

After all such $k$ have been processed in row $i$, if $W_{ii}=0$, return
`zero-pivot(i)`. Otherwise the upper row entries $U_{ij}$ are the current
$W_{ij}$ for $(i,j)\in P$ and $j\ge i$. Continue to the next row.

If every row completes, return `ok` with the unit-lower factor $L$ (stored
strict-lower entries $L_{ik}=W_{ik}$ for $(i,k)\in P$) and the upper factor
$U$ (stored entries $U_{ij}=W_{ij}$ for $(i,j)\in P$, $j\ge i$). Both factors
use only positions in $P$; the diagonal of $L$ is implicit, and all other
unstored off-diagonal entries are zero. The numeric values remain stored at
their structural slots if an update makes a value zero.

For a successful factor pair and $r\in F^n$, apply the preconditioner as
follows. For $i=1,\ldots,n$ in order, initialize $y_i:=r_i$ and, for each
$k<i$ with $(i,k)\in P$ in increasing order, update
$y_i:=y_i-L_{ik}y_k$. Then for $i=n,n-1,\ldots,1$, initialize $x_i:=y_i$;
for each $k>i$ with $(i,k)\in P$ in decreasing order, update
$x_i:=x_i-U_{ik}x_k$; finally set $x_i:=x_i/U_{ii}$. Visit every such stored
factor slot exactly once, including slots whose current factor value is zero.
These are the forward and backward substitution recurrences, with their sums
traversed only over stored strict-triangular slots. The pivot checks ensure
every denominator in this application is nonzero. This procedure defines setup
and application only; it asserts no factorization identity $A=LU$, Krylov
convergence, conditioning improvement, or accuracy guarantee.

derivations.claim: The input has finite arrays and $n$ is finite. Validation visits the $n$ row intervals and $s$ stored entries once; the factorization loops over at most $n$ rows, finitely many pattern entries, and finite row-list merges. Every division is preceded by a nonzero-pivot check, and [A1] makes each such division defined. Thus the procedure either returns one of its specified failure statuses or completes with `ok`.

If the procedure returns `ok`, each processed pivot is nonzero by its check, so the returned $U$ has nonzero diagonal. The definition sets $L$ to be unit lower triangular and retains only upper entries in $U$.

Initially the work values occupy exactly the input slots $P$. Each multiplier is written only at a strict-lower slot in $P_L$, and each update is performed only when both matching row positions are in $P$. No update allocates a new position. Induction over the finite row and pivot loops therefore gives stored patterns $P_L$ and $P_U$ for $L$ and $U$, respectively.

The forward recurrence in [F3] applied to unit-lower $L$ and the backward recurrence in [F4] applied to $U$ are well-defined because $L_{ii}=1$ and every $U_{ii}\ne0$. By [F5] and [F6] they produce the unique successive triangular-solve outputs specified by the algorithm.

The sets $P_L$ and $P_U$ are disjoint and partition $P$: every $(i,j)\in P$ has exactly one of $i>j$ or $i\le j$. Hence $\ell+q=|P|=s$. Since the unit diagonal of $L$ is implicit, this is exactly the factor numeric-slot count.

On success, the outer lower-pattern loop processes every one of the $\ell$ positions once and performs one division there. For a fixed $(i,k)\in P_L$, the update loop visits exactly the indices in $R_{ik}\cap C_k$; each visit performs one multiplication and one subtraction. Summing these counts gives exactly $\ell$ divisions and $I$ multiplications and subtractions.

Both lists in each intersection are strictly increasing. A two-pointer merge advances at least one pointer at every comparison and stops when one list ends, so it makes at most the sum of the two list lengths, $|R_{ik}|+|C_k|$, comparisons. Summing over $P_L$ gives the bound $J$; validation visits each row interval and stored entry once.

The forward recurrence in [F3] performs one multiplication and subtraction for each stored strict-lower slot, hence $\ell$ of each and no diagonal divisions. The backward recurrence in [F4] performs one multiplication and subtraction for each stored strict-upper slot, hence $u$ of each, and one division for each of its $n$ rows. Since $\ell+u=\ell+q-n=s-n$, the stated application counts follow.

derivations.claim: By [F4], the displayed matrix entries are in a field. Its nonzero pattern is the diagonal together with the four adjacent off-diagonal positions. It is canonical, sorted by column in every row, and contains all three diagonal positions, so the algorithm has no input-pattern or missing-diagonal failure.

In row 1 the factors are $U_{11}=4$ and $U_{12}=-1$. In row 2 the multiplier is $L_{21}=-1/4$; the matching update at column 2 gives $U_{22}=4-(-1/4)(-1)=15/4$. The row-2 entry at column 3 remains $U_{23}=-1$ because row 1 has no position at column 3.

Row 3 has no position at column 1. Its multiplier at column 2 is $L_{32}=(-1)/(15/4)=-4/15$. The matching update at column 3 gives $U_{33}=4-(-4/15)(-1)=56/15$. All three pivots are nonzero, so the procedure returns `ok` with the displayed factors.

derivations.claim: Take $$A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&0\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$ By [F4], this is a matrix over a field. Its canonical sorted CSR pattern is $P=\{(1,1),(1,2),(2,2),(3,1),(3,3)\}$, with all diagonal entries equal to $1$. Thus the input satisfies the algorithm's domain and has no missing diagonal.

The first row gives $U_{11}=U_{12}=1$. Row 2 has no strict-lower position and gives $U_{22}=1$. In row 3 the only strict-lower position is $(3,1)$, so $L_{31}=1$. The update from this multiplier can reach only a column $j>1$ present in both row 3 and row 1; no such column exists. Hence $L_{32}$ is not stored, $U_{33}=1$, and the procedure returns `ok` with $$L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad U=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
By [F3], $(LU)_{32}=L_{31}U_{12}+L_{32}U_{22}+L_{33}U_{32}=1$, whereas $A_{32}=0$. Therefore $LU$ has a nonzero outside the input pattern, so the refuted statement is false.

derivations.claim: Since this run reaches the first step, [F1] gives $r_0\ne0$ and $\beta=\sqrt{\langle r_0,r_0\rangle}>0$. Since $\beta$ is real, $\langle r_0/\beta,r_0/\beta\rangle=\beta^{-2}\langle r_0,r_0\rangle=1$, so $v_1$ has norm $1$. Inductively suppose $v_1,\ldots,v_j$ are orthonormal. At the $i$th Gram–Schmidt substep, the current vector $w$ is orthogonal to $v_k$ for $k<i$. The update $w':=w-h_{ij}v_i$, with $h_{ij}=\langle w,v_i\rangle$, satisfies $\langle w',v_i\rangle=h_{ij}-h_{ij}\langle v_i,v_i\rangle=0$ and $\langle w',v_k\rangle=\langle w,v_k\rangle-h_{ij}\langle v_i,v_k\rangle=0$ for each $k<i$. These equalities use linearity in the first argument and orthonormality [F4]. After all $i=1,\ldots,j$, the final $w$ is orthogonal to every current basis vector. Nonbreakdown gives $h_{j+1,j}=\|w\|_2>0$; the same inner-product calculation gives $\langle v_{j+1},v_{j+1}\rangle=h_{j+1,j}^{-2}\langle w,w\rangle=1$, and its orthogonality follows from that of $w$. Induction proves orthonormality through $v_{m+1}$.

The finite matrix $\bar H_m$ defines a linear map $\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb C^{m+1}$ between finite-dimensional inner-product spaces by [F6], [F10], and [F11]. By [F7], least-squares minimizers exist and any two differ by an element of $\ker\bar H_m$. This kernel is zero: if $\bar H_my=0$, its zero-based last row $a=m$ gives $h_{m+1,m}y_{m-1}=0$, hence $y_{m-1}=0$. For each one-based row label $r=m,m-1,\ldots,2$ in descending order, matrix row $r-1$ has coefficient $h_{r,r-1}$ in column $r-2$; its other possibly nonzero terms use coordinates $y_{k-1}$ with $k\ge r$, already shown zero. Thus $h_{r,r-1}y_{r-2}=0$. Since $h_{r,r-1}=h_{(r-1)+1,r-1}>0$ by no breakdown, we obtain $y_{r-2}=0$. Thus every zero-based coordinate vanishes, $\bar H_m$ is injective, and its least-squares minimizer is unique.

At the end of column $j$, the successive subtractions give $Az_j=\sum_{i=1}^j h_{ij}v_i+w$. Since $w=h_{j+1,j}v_{j+1}$, this is $Az_j=\sum_{i=1}^{j+1}h_{ij}v_i$. Assembling these column identities for $j=1,\ldots,m$ yields $AZ_m=V_{m+1}\bar H_m$.

The initial residual is $r_0=b-Ax_0=\beta v_1$. The vector $e_0$ has value $1$ in coordinate $0$ and $0$ in every other coordinate by [F11], so $V_{m+1}\beta e_0=\beta v_1$. For any $y\in\mathbb C^m$, linearity and step 1.3 give $b-A(x_0+Z_my)=r_0-AZ_my=V_{m+1}(\beta e_0-\bar H_my)$.

For every $c\in\mathbb C^{m+1}$, orthonormality from step 1.1 and the coordinate inner product [F4] give $\|V_{m+1}c\|_2^2=\langle V_{m+1}c,V_{m+1}c\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}\sum_{k=1}^{m+1}c_{i-1}\overline{c_{k-1}}\langle v_i,v_k\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}|c_{i-1}|^2=\|c\|_2^2$. Taking the nonnegative square roots defined by [F5] proves norm preservation. Apply it to $c=\beta e_0-\bar H_my$ in step 2.1 to obtain the asserted norm identity.

Put $S=\{z_1,\ldots,z_m\}$. By [F9], every $u\in\operatorname{span}(S)$ is a finite combination $u=\sum_{a<q}c_a z_{j_a}$ for some $q\in\mathbb N$, where $a$ is a zero-based list coordinate and each $j_a\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ is a one-based column label. For each one-based column label $k=1,\ldots,m$, define the zero-based coordinate $y_{k-1}$ of $y\in\mathbb C^m$ to be $\sum_{a<q,\ j_a=k}c_a$, taking this empty sum to be zero. The finite sum laws and distributivity give $u=\sum_{k=1}^m y_{k-1}z_k=Z_my$ by the column convention in the algorithm. Conversely, each $Z_my$ is the finite linear combination $\sum_{k=1}^m y_{k-1}z_k$, so it lies in $\operatorname{span}(S)$ by [F8] and [F9]. Thus the two sets agree. By step 3.1, for every vector in this affine set its true residual norm equals $\|\beta e_0-\bar H_my\|_2$. Therefore the unique least-squares minimizer from step 1.2 gives $x_m=x_0+Z_my_m$ with minimum true residual over the whole affine span.
